The

of

Her

and

time

Rivard

She

As

[5]

Nothing

that

Rivard

was

anything

an

worker.

She

no

[6]

Counsel

that

I

dant.

That

ed.

The

was

in

a

contractual

one.

It

true

that

tation

the

The

company

employment

and

prac

tices

"Revised:

September

21,

1984".

Rivard

Hitachi.

[7]

Simply

while

a

contract

employment,

I

agreement

the

that

bears

reasonable

notice.

[8]

In

mid-October

1985

Rivard

became

sick

at

work.

She

relates

There

Although

[9]

I

pause

note,

that

because

of

her

illness

Rivard

not

six

note,

5,

1985,

I

1985

nor

Rivard,

As

notice

It

Employment

1987,

E-110,

Hitachi

Rivard

entitled

six

[14]

Before

proceeding

further,

I

will

comment

more

fully

upon

the

impression

that

Rivard

made

upon

me.

In

general

terms,

I

must

say

that

her

following

the

end

her

employment

was,

having

consideration

for

her

illness,

somewhat

odd.

From

the

and

from

my

own

observations,

I

am

left

with

considerable

confusion

about

her

the

that

she

is

trying

to

what

an

unfortunate

[15]

In

the

months

next

following

the

Rivard

no

the

In

11,

1985,

She

As

[17]

At

ance

After

ployment

Her

[18]

Almost

one

year

after

the

termina

tion,

on

September

15,

1986,

Rivard

issued

two

separate

statements

of

claim

against

Hitachi.

In

the

first,

she

claimed

damages

for

personal

injury

alleged

to

have

been

sustained

in

the

course

her

employment

and

to

have

been

caused

by

her

employer's

negli

gence.

In

the

second,

she

alleged

unjust

dismissal

and

lack

of

proper

notice.

Following

commencement

of

the

actions,

it

was

the

personal

injury

claim

that

appears

to

have

received

most

of

her

attention.

[19]

I

do

not

intend

to

review

what

transpired

in

that

latter

proceeding,

except

to

note

that

the

principal

issue

was

whether

Hitachi

was

an

employer

covered

by

the

Workers'

Compensation

Act,

R.S.M.

1987,

c.

W-200,

and

whether

the

plaintiff

had

any

independent

right

of

action

against

it.

That

issue

required

participation

by

the

Workers'

Compensation

Board

itself

and

involved

an

application

for

certiorari.

The

Court

of

Appeal

of

Manitoba

ultimately

confirmed

that

the

plaintiff

had

no

remedy

other

than

through

Workers'

Compensation

in

respect

of

her

alleged

work-related

illness.

[20]

With

that

question

resolved,

the

plaintiff

then

seems

to

have

focused

her

attention

on

the

wrongful

dismissal

action.

Although

what

she

seeks

in

this

proceeding

is

compensation

in

lieu

of

reasonable

notice,

it

is

quite

apparent

that

what

she

really

wants

is

the

same

damages

which

she

had

hoped

to

recover

in

the

other

action,

but

which

she

is

precluded

by

law

from

pursuing.

There

can

be

no

substance

to

this

"backdoor"

approach

to

assessing

her

claim.

Even

if

it

had

been

proved

in

the

trial

before

me

that

Rivard

lost

six

months

of

earnings

because

of

her

exposure

to

lacquer

spray,

that

would

have

no

bearing

whatsoever

on

the

determination

of

the

payment

to

which

she

was

entitled

in

lieu

of

notice.

[21]

I

have

compared

the

basic

facts

of

this

case

to

those

in

some

of

the

decisions

cited

in

Harris's

text,

Wrongful

Dismissal

and

Butterworths'

Wrongful

Dismissal

Practice

Manual.

That

is,

I

have

looked

at

cases

where

the

employees

in

question

were

of

similar

age,

in

similar

job

situations

and

had

similar

periods

of

service.

It

quickly

became

obvious

that

when

one

considers

employees

who

are

nonprofes

sional,

non-managerial

and

young

and

who

have

had

relatively

short

terms

of

employment,

comparisons

are

of

little

value

or

assistance.

[22]

Furthermore,

it

was

made.

quite

clear

by

our

Court

of

Appeal,

in

Yosyk

et

al.

v.

Westfair

Foods

Ltd.

et

al.

(1988),

51

Man.R.(2d)

191
,

that

a

purely

comparative

approach

is

not

the

appropriate

way

to

determine

reasonable

notice.

[23]

After

referring

to

Lazarowicz

v.

Orenda

Engines

Ltd.,

[1961]

0.R.

141;

Gilman

v.

Winnipeg

Board

of

Jewish

Education

(1986),

39

Man.R.(2d)

21
,

and

Balchin

v.

Diecast

Morwest

Ltd.

(1987),

46

Man.R.(2d)

201
,

Twaddle,

J.A.,

concluded

that

the

determination

of

what

is

reasonable

is

not

a

purely

subjective

matter.

Rather,

reasonable

ness

is

something

that

must

be

objec

tively

determined,

"having

regard

to

the

intention

of

the

parties".

In

so

saying,

Justice

Twaddle

made

clear

that,

because

the

relationship

between

an

employer

and

employee

is

not

a

static

one,

the

intention

of

the

parties

as

to

the

length

of

notice

required

by

either

to

end

their

rela

tionship

may

change

from

time

to

time

as

the

employment

goes

on.

[24]

Mr.

Houston

argued

that

to

call

on

a

court

to

ascertain

intention

when

none

was

expressed

is

nothing

more

than

an

invitation

to

engage

in

fanciful

speculation.

I

have,

however,

rejected

his

argument.

It

is

not

uncommon

for

courts

to

read

missing

terms

into

contracts,

provided,

of

course,

that

in

so

doing

the

conclusion

has

a

basis

in

the

evidence.

[25]

The

relevant

evidence

before

this

court

is

as

follows:

Hitachi

employees

received

salary

adjustments

in

December

of

each

year;

in

December

of

1984,

at

the

beginning

of

Rivard's

last

year

of

employment,

she

received

a

5.1%

in

crease;

this

adjustment

was

consistent

with

the

general

increases

in

salary

which

she

had

received

since

the

date

of

her

employment,

but

did

not

indicate

any

promotion

or

significant

upgrading.

[26]

There

is

no

evidence

that

over

the

period

which

Rivard

spent

with

Hitachi

her

work

had

become

more

difficult

or

her

responsibilities

greater.

As

I

have

already

said,

there

appears

to

have

been

little

supervision

of

her

work

and

nothing,

except

for

after-the-event

reports,

to

suggest

that

she

was

anything

better

or

worse

than

a

normal

clerical

employee.

[27]

I

am

quite

certain

that

if,

prior

to

the

autumn

of

1985,

Rivard

and

Hitachi

had

addressed

the

question

of

termination

notice,

they

would

have

assumed

that

the

relationship

which

existed

between

them

was

fairly

stable,

but

with

little

prospect

of

advancement

other

than

incremental

salary

in

creases.

While

both

would

have

treated

the

job

as

one

with

reasonable

secur

ity,

neither

would

have

been

likely

to

agree

to

a

lengthy

period

of

notice

prior

to

termination.

Conversely,

both

would

have

assumed

that

a

person

with

Rivard's

experience

and

relatively

young

age

would

have

little

difficulty

finding

alternative

employment

within

a

fairly

short

time

frame.

In

fact,

once

Rivard

was

well

enough

to

work,

she

found

a

new

job

quickly.

[28]

With

the

foregoing

factors

in

mind,

I

have

applied

the

test

suggested

by

Mr.

Justice

Twaddle

and

have

reached

the

conclusion

that

from

the

point

of

view

of

both

Rivard

and

Hitachi

it

would

be

reasonable

to

read

into

the

unwritten

contract

of

employment

a

notice

provision

of

eight

weeks.

It

may

be

of

interest,

but

of

no

great

importance,

to

observe

that

my

conclu

sion

falls

within

the

same

range

as

other

decisions

where

the

facts

appear

to

be

roughly

similar.

[29]

At

the

time

of

Rivard's

termina

tion

she

was

being

paid

$325.00

per

week.

Since

she

has

already

received

payment

for

four

weeks

in

lieu

of

notice,

she

will

now

have

judgment

for

$1,300.00,

being

the

equivalent

of

a

further

four

weeks'

salary.

[30]

I

received

no

submissions

with

to

costs.

I

that,

while

the

plaintiff

is

her
